content: Turpentine, also referred to as spirit of turpentine, oil of turpentine, wood turpentine, or gum turpentine, is a liquid derived through the distillation of resin obtained from trees, primarily pine trees. Its chemical composition predominantly consists of terpenes, with alpha-pinene and beta-pinene being the main monoterpenes present. Turpentine has a strong, pungent odor that is often likened to the smell of nail polish remover. Colloquially, it is sometimes called turps, though this term more commonly refers to turpentine substitutes, such as mineral turpentine. The term turpentine originates from the Greek word terebinthine, which refers to the terebinth tree, a species from which the substance was originally distilled. Historically, one of the earliest sources of turpentine was the terebinth tree (Pistacia terebinthus), a Mediterranean species related to the pistachio tree. Today, important pine species used for turpentine production include the Maritime Pine (Pinus pinaster), Aleppo Pine (Pinus halepensis), Masson’s Pine (Pinus massoniana), Sumatran Pine (Pinus merkusii), Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris), Loblolly Pine (Pinus taeda), and Ponderosa Pine (Pinus ponderosa). Industrial Uses Turpentine is primarily utilized in industry as a solvent and as a source of raw materials for organic synthesis. As a solvent, it is employed for thinning oil-based paints, producing varnishes, and serving as a raw material in the chemical industry. However, in industrialized nations, its use as a solvent has largely been replaced by cheaper turpentine substitutes derived from crude oil. Specialized forms of turpentine include Canada balsam (also known as Canada turpentine or balsam of fir), which is made from the resin of the balsam fir, and Venice turpentine, which is derived from the Western Larch (Larix occidentalis). Turpentine is also a key raw material in the synthesis of fragrant chemical compounds. Commercially important products such as camphor, linalool, alpha-terpineol, and geraniol are typically synthesized from alpha-pinene and beta-pinene, the primary chemical components of turpentine. These pinenes are separated and purified through distillation. The residue left after turpentine distillation, which contains a mixture of diterpenes and triterpenes, is sold as rosin. Additionally, turpentine is incorporated into various cleaning and sanitary products due to its antiseptic properties and its characteristic clean scent. Medicinal Uses Turpentine has been used medicinally since ancient times. When applied externally, it is an effective treatment for lice infestations. It can also be mixed with animal fat to create a rudimentary chest rub for alleviating nasal and throat ailments, similar to modern products like Vicks VapoRub. Historically, turpentine was administered internally to treat intestinal parasites due to its antiseptic and diuretic properties. However, internal use of turpentine is no longer common practice today. Ingesting turpentine is extremely dangerous and can be life-threatening. Furthermore, consuming turpentine is not a safe or effective method for inducing abortion. Hazards Turpentine, as an organic solvent, poses significant health and safety risks similar to those of other solvents. Its natural origin does not make it less harmful than synthetic alternatives. Inhalation of turpentine vapor can irritate the skin and eyes, damage the lungs and respiratory system, and affect the central nervous system. Ingestion of turpentine can lead to renal failure and other severe health complications. Additionally, turpentine is highly flammable, further increasing its potential hazards.
